result:
Good — everything I touched is staged, both suites are green, and nothing else was swept in.

I did the capture, and it changed the plan a little.

The literal ask — screenshot the farm, then recolor it in an image editor for "warmer" and "cooler" — is exactly what the look rig's own rule forbids: it can only compare looks the game can actually draw, so nobody picks a color the engine hasn't proven it can render. So instead of a fake recolor, I gave the world a real warm/cool switch: same trick the day/night sky already uses (one color multiply over the whole screen), just a second color layered onto that. It costs nothing extra at runtime and defaults to invisible — if nobody touches this axis, the game renders pixel-for-pixel as it does today.

Then I ran it for real: day 3, 9:30 AM, seed 12345, her and the well in frame, a few crops at different growth stages so the grade has more than bare dirt to sit on. Three genuine frames came out — as it ships, warmer, cooler — same moment, same everything else. I checked the actual pixels moved in the right direction and by an amount you can actually see, not just in theory.

One honest side effect worth knowing: the top HUD bar's background rides the same color wash as the world — it already does this for the existing day/night tint, I just inherited it rather than caused it. The numbers and icons stay perfectly readable; only the bar's background shade drifts with the grade, same as it already drifts from dawn to dusk.

Both test suites are green (1983 unit, 528 integration). Unrelated finding, not something to fix here: the visual-regression tool fails in this sandbox even with zero code changes — a rendering-driver mismatch against whatever machine captured the baseline, not a real regression. That's the same gap already sitting in "Give the visual check a home, or stop claiming it" — no new item needed.

I tried to hand you a page with the three frames side by side, and publishing got declined — this looks like a worker session with nobody present to approve sending anything to Anthropic's servers, the same shape of limit as not being able to launch Godot from chat, just for a different step. The frames themselves are real, sitting in this worktree; whoever runs the next step ("bring the four looks back for the pick") can publish them properly.
